power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Identifying predictors of differential treatment benefit of the digital intervention priovi for borderline personality disorder: a model-based recursive partitioning analysis
table.research_questions:
1) Which baseline patient characteristics moderate the treatment effect of priovi on borderline symptom severity, operationalized as a change in BSL-23 sum score at the primary follow-up time point T1 (3 months)?
2) Which baseline patient characteristics moderate the effect of priovi on rate of clinically relevant response at T1 (3 months)? Primary hypothesis (non-directional; confirmatory): We hypothesize that the treatment effect of priovi on change in BSL-23 sum score at T1 is heterogeneous with respect to at least one of the split variables listed under Measured variables. The primary hypothesis is non-directional, in line with the data-adaptive nature of the method.
The primary hypothesis is supported for a given outcome if (i) the omnibus pmtest() rejects at alpha = 0.05 and (ii) at least one candidate split variable shows a non-zero conditional permutation importance with corresponding subgroup CATEs whose 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (see Inference criteria) exclude zero and differ between subgroups in the representative tree.

Secondary hypothesis A (non-directional; confirmatory, unless the primary hypothesis is not supported, in which case this hypothesis will be regarded exploratory): We hypothesize that the treatment effect of priovi on the probability of being classified as a responder at T1 is heterogeneous with respect to at least one of the split variables listed under Measured variables. This secondary hypothesis is non-directional, in line with the data-adaptive nature of the method.

Secondary hypothesis B (directional, theory-anchored): Among the seven candidate split variables, we hold a directional prior for variables that index baseline psychopathology severity – baseline BSL-23, PHQ-9, GAD-7 sum scores, and number of suicide attempts and life-threatening events in the 3 months before baseline – such that higher values are expected to be associated with larger absolute treatment benefit (i.e., larger reduction in BSL-23; higher probability of being classified as a responder). For psychotherapy status and medication status at baseline, we do not pre-specify a direction. 
The secondary directional hypothesis will be evaluated descriptively, conditional on the primary hypothesis being supported: for each of the directionally pre-specified variables that emerges as influential by the conditional permutation importance, the CATE in the subgroup with higher psychopathology values is compared to the CATE in the corresponding lower-psychopathology subgroup of the representative tree. A finding that contradicts the pre-specified direction will be reported transparently but will not be interpreted as confirming the secondary hypothesis.
table.datasets_used:
The analysis will be performed as a secondary analysis on data from the EPADIP-BPD RCT. The RCT included 580 participants with diagnosis of borderline personality disorder, assessed via SCID-5-PD, at least moderate symptom severity (BSL-23 >= 1.07), without comorbid substance use disorder or psychotic disorder. 302 participants were randomized to the intervention group, receiving access to priovi in addition to treatment as usual, and 278 were randomized to the control group, receiving access to treatment as usual only. 
Measurement time points were at baseline (T0) and after 3 (T1), 6 (T2) and 12 (T3) months. The primary time point for analysis of effectiveness of priovi was T1 (3 months); accordingly, T1 will also be the primary time point of the present secondary analysis. The analyses at T2 and T3 will be performed as exploratory sensitivity analyses to assess stability of identified moderators over time.
All participants of the EPADIP-RCT who took part in the respective follow-up time point of interest will be included in the planned analysis. 
Variables of interest for the present analyses are: borderline symptom severity (BSL-23) at baseline (T0) and follow-up (T1/T2/T3), baseline depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), baseline anxiety symptoms (GAD-7), number of suicide attempts in past 3 months before baseline, number of life-threatening events in past 3 months at baseline, psychotherapy status at baseline, medication status at baseline. 

The dataset is described in detail in the main publication (Assmann et al., 2025).

table.measured_variables:
Outcome measures:
- Borderline symptom severity (change in BSL-23 sum score from T0 to T1, with changes to T2 and T3 as exploratory time points); continuous
- Responder status (responders are defined by both reaching the psychometric criterion of a reliable change index and having a change in the total score of BSL-23 towards a less severe grade from baseline); binary: 1 (responder) / 0 (non-responder)

Baseline covariate (used in the base model, see Statistical models):
- Borderline symptom severity (BSL-23 sum score at T0); continuous

Candidate split-variables (potential moderators of the treatment effect):
- baseline borderline symptom severity (BSL-23 sum score at T0); continuous
- baseline depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 sum score at T0); continuous
- baseline anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 sum score at T0); continuous
- number of suicide attempts in the 3 months before baseline; continuous (count)
- number of life-threatening events in the 3 months before baseline; continuous (count)
- psychotherapy status at baseline; binary: 1 (psychotherapy) / 0 (no psychotherapy)
- medication status (intake of sedatives or antidepressants) at baseline; binary: 1 (medication) / 0 (no medication)


Note that baseline BSL-23 at T0 enters the analysis in two roles: (i) as a covariate in the base models for the BSL-23 outcome, to adjust for regression to the mean, and (ii) as a candidate split variable, allowing the recursive partitioning to identify whether the treatment effect is moderated by baseline severity. This is a deliberate choice: the splitting is performed on the score-based instability of the treatment effect parameter across baseline BSL-23 values, not on its mean level.
table.missing_data_handling:
Out of 302 participants randomized to the IG, 35 (11.59%) did not complete the T1 assessment after 3 months, 53 (17.55%) did not complete the T2 assessment after 6 months, 67 (22.19%) did not complete the T3 assessment after 12 months.
Out of 278 participants randomized to the CG, 15 (5.4%) did not complete the T1 assessment, 23 (8.27%) did not complete the T2 assessment, and 60 (21.58%) did not complete the T3 assessment. Dropout is therefore differential across groups, with somewhat higher drop-out in the intervention group.

All analyses are conducted on a complete-case basis: at each follow-up time point, the analysis is restricted to the participants who provided an observed outcome at that time point. Missing outcomes are not imputed. Because complete T0 data was a prerequisite for randomization, baseline BSL-23 and all seven candidate split variables are fully observed; the only missingness occurs in the outcome variable at the respective follow-up time point. Complete-case analysis therefore simply excludes the participants with a missing outcome at that time point and retains all observed information on the remaining participants. This yields analysis samples of N = 530 at T1 (the primary, confirmatory time point), N = 504 at T2, and N = 453 at T3 (see Unit of analysis). Because dropout is differential across arms (see above), complete-case estimates rest on the assumption that outcome missingness is conditionally ignorable given randomization arm and the observed baseline variables; we report the observed per-arm completion rates transparently and treat the differential dropout as a limitation in the interpretation of the findings. Uncertainty for the reported estimates (subgroup treatment effects, variable importance scores, and the validation metrics) is quantified by a nonparametric bootstrap on the complete-case data, as described under Statistical models.
table.unit_of_analysis:
Consistent with the complete-case strategy described under Missing data, each analysis includes the participants who contributed an observed outcome at the relevant follow-up time point: 530 (267 IG, 263 CG) at T1 (the primary, confirmatory analysis), 504 (249 IG, 255 CG) at T2, and 453 (235 IG, 218 CG) at T3. Participants with a missing outcome at a given time point are excluded from the analysis at that time point only.

Note: complete T0 data was a prerequisite for randomization; therefore all participants have non-missing values on baseline BSL-23 and on all candidate split variables, and only the outcome variable at the respective follow-up time point is subject to missingness and thus determines complete-case inclusion.

table.statistical_tests:
To identify combinations of baseline variables that moderate the treatment effect of priovi, we will use model-based recursive partitioning (Seibold et al., 2016, 2018). This approach combines a parametric base model for the treatment effect with a non-parametric, data-adaptive search for subgroups in which the treatment-effect parameter is unstable across candidate moderators. Both outcomes are analysed separately at the primary time point T1, and the same modelling pipeline is then repeated at T2 and T3 as exploratory sensitivity analyses (see Exploratory analysis).

The analyses rely on two outcome-specific base models, in which the group (treatment) parameter is the parameter of primary interest for partitioning. For the continuous outcome (change in BSL-23 from T0 to T1), the base model is a baseline-corrected ANCOVA, lm(delta_bsl23 ~ bsl23_T0 + group), which adjusts the estimated treatment effect for regression to the mean. For the binary responder outcome, the base model is a bias-reduced logistic regression, glm(responder ~ group, family = binomial("logit"), method = "brglmFit"), fitted with the brglm2 package. We chose bias-reduced logistic regression over standard maximum-likelihood logistic regression because brglmFit yields finite, well-defined coefficient estimates even under near-separation conditions that may occur in small terminal nodes with extreme responder rates, while remaining virtually identical to standard maximum likelihood in the absence of separation. Because brglm2 objects inherit from glm, the score function and information matrix used by model4you::pmforest() for parameter-instability testing remain available.

For each outcome, we fit a model-based random forest with model4you::pmforest() using the corresponding base model. The seven candidate split variables described under Measured variables are passed to the forest via zformula = ~ bsl23_T0 + phq9_T0 + gad7_T0 + suicide_attempts_T0 + life_threatening_events_T0 + psychotherapy_T0 + medication_T0. Each forest consists of 500 trees (ntree = 500) grown on subsamples of size 0.632·N drawn without replacement (perturb = list(replace = FALSE, fraction = 0.632)) and stratified by group (strata = group), so that the treatment-arm balance is preserved in every subsample. At each split, three candidate variables are randomly selected (mtry = 3), and partitioning is governed by ctree_control(teststat = "quad", testtype = "Univ", mincriterion = 0, minbucket = 50, lookahead = TRUE, saveinfo = FALSE). The combination of minbucket = 50 with stratified resampling is intended to keep the treatment-effect parameter stable and to limit overfitting: given the observed arm balance of 52.1%/47.9% (302 IG vs. 278 CG) and the fact that all candidate split variables are independent of group at baseline by randomization, the probability of any terminal node containing fewer than 15 observations in either arm is approximately 0.3% per node.

For each outcome, four sets of results will be reported. First, we test the global null hypothesis of no treatment-effect heterogeneity across the candidate split variables using the omnibus parametric-bootstrap test model4you::pmtest() with B = 1000 bootstrap replicates. To clarify the role of the two resampling schemes in this pipeline: parameter instability itself is assessed at every potential split inside each tree by a deterministic score-based M-fluctuation test on the base-model score residuals, and the ensemble of 500 trees stabilises the resulting variable-selection signal and treatment-effect estimates by averaging over stratified subsamples; the B = 1000 parametric-bootstrap replicates in pmtest() (under which new outcome values are simulated from the fitted base model rather than permuted) are used solely to construct the null reference distribution against which the observed forest-level instability statistic is compared in order to obtain the omnibus p-value. Second, we quantify the relative contribution of each candidate split variable using conditional permutation variable importance (Strobl et al., 2008), computed via model4you::varimp() with conditional = TRUE, OOB = TRUE, nperm = 5, and threshold = 0.2. The conditional version of the importance measure is used to adjust for correlations among candidate split variables, which are expected to be substantial between baseline BSL-23, PHQ-9, and GAD-7 sum scores; for comparison and transparency, unconditional importance (conditional = FALSE) will additionally be reported in the supplement. Third, to obtain an interpretable summary of the moderating structure, we fit a single representative MOB tree to the full dataset using model4you::pmtree() with the same base model and the same zformula, but with testtype = "Bonferroni", mincriterion = 0.95, and minbucket = 50. Fourth, for the three candidate split variables with the highest conditional permutation importance, we will produce partial dependence plots that display the predicted conditional average treatment effect (CATE) as a function of each moderator while averaging over the empirical distribution of the remaining variables.

The entire MOB-RP pipeline described above is fitted once to the complete-case dataset for each outcome at each follow-up time point. Specifically, we (i) fit the model-based forest with pmforest() and the corresponding base model, (ii) compute the omnibus heterogeneity p-value with pmtest() (B = 1000 parametric-bootstrap replicates), (iii) compute conditional permutation variable importance scores with varimp(), and (iv) fit a single representative MOB tree to the complete-case dataset with pmtree() (testtype = "Bonferroni", mincriterion = 0.95, minbucket = 50). The omnibus p-value from pmtest(), the point estimates and rank order of the conditional permutation importance scores, and the representative tree are read directly from this single fit.

To attach uncertainty to the importance scores and to the subgroup treatment effects without relying on distributional assumptions, we use a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples participants with replacement, stratified by randomization arm to preserve the arm balance (B = 1000 bootstrap resamples). In each bootstrap resample we (a) refit the forest and recompute the conditional permutation variable importance scores, and (b) re-estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) within each subgroup defined by the representative tree fitted on the original complete-case dataset. The tree structure is defined once on the original complete-case data and held fixed; the bootstrap re-evaluates these fixed subgroups so that the reported subgroup CATEs and their 95% confidence intervals reflect sampling variability while keeping the interpretation anchored to a single, reportable tree. For each importance score and each subgroup CATE, the 95% confidence interval is obtained from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its bootstrap distribution. As a stability summary, we additionally refit the representative tree in each bootstrap resample and report the empirical frequency with which each candidate split variable is selected at the root split.

Fallback for computational cost. The pre-specified pipeline (per outcome and per follow-up time point: one 500-tree forest, a 1,000-replicate pmtest(), and a 1,000-resample stratified nonparametric bootstrap in which the forest is refit and the conditional variable importance recomputed) is computationally demanding, and we will run it as specified whenever feasible on the available compute. If the analysis proves computationally intractable in practice, we will apply, in a single pre-specified step, the following reduction: ntree is lowered from 500 to 200, the number of parametric-bootstrap replicates B in pmtest() is lowered from 1,000 to 200, and the number of nonparametric bootstrap resamples is lowered from 1,000 to 500. All other settings (mtry, perturb, strata, the ctree_control parameters, and minbucket) remain unchanged, as does the pooling of bootstrap percentile confidence intervals. If this fallback is triggered, it is applied consistently to both outcomes and to all follow-up time points, and its use is transparently reported in the final paper.

All analyses will be performed in R (≥ 4.4) using the packages model4you (≥ 0.9-8) (Seibold et al., 2019), partykit (Hothorn & Zeileis, 2015), brglm2 (Kosmidis, 2017), and ggplot2 (Wickham, 2011). The forest fitting and the nonparametric bootstrap will be parallelised across cores to keep the pipeline tractable. To ensure exact reproducibility, set.seed(1234) is fixed before the analysis is initiated and propagated to the bootstrap resampling; the package versions, the random seed, and the full analysis script will be deposited on OSF together with this preregistration.
table.statistical_power:
Closed-form power calculations for model-based recursive partitioning are not available because the procedure is data-adaptive (splits, depth, and node sizes are estimated from the data). We therefore quantify expected power using a heuristic anchor based on classical interaction power calculations. 

Following (Brookes et al., 2004), detecting a treatment × moderator interaction of the same standardized magnitude as a main effect requires approximately four times the sample size to attain the same power. Given the average treatment effect of priovi at T1 reported in the main publication (Cohen's d = 0.24 on BSL-23), we anchor the expected power for the present subgroup analyses on this value. 

Because the confirmatory analysis is performed on a complete-case basis, the relevant sample size for the T1 analysis is the complete-case N of 530 (267 IG, 263 CG), on which we anchor the power calculation.

Specifically, with N = 530 (267 IG, 263 CG) at T1, the present sample provides:

- approximately 80% power to detect a between-subgroup difference in the standardized treatment effect of d = 0.25 at uncorrected alpha = 0.05;
- approximately 80% power to detect a between-subgroup difference of d = 0.35 after Bonferroni correction across the seven candidate split variables (alpha = 0.05 / 7 = 0.0071), as applied within the recursive partitioning splitting rule.

Smaller heterogeneity (e.g., a subgroup contrast of d ≤ 0.15) is unlikely to be reliably detected with the present sample. We therefore interpret the present analysis as well-powered for moderately sized effect heterogeneity (subgroup contrasts of d ≥ 0.35 in the standardized treatment effect) and underpowered for smaller heterogeneity.
table.inference_criteria:
All confirmatory tests are two-tailed, in accordance with the non-directional primary hypothesis (see Hypotheses). The nominal significance level is alpha = 0.05.

The forest uses unadjusted p-values with mincriterion = 0 to maximize variable-importance signal.

In the representative tree, model-based recursive partitioning performs two-tailed score-based parameter-instability (M-fluctuation) tests at each split. To rigorously control the family-wise error rate during the recursive partitioning process, p-values for potential splits are adjusted using a Bonferroni correction over the seven candidate split variables. 

Across outcomes: the two outcomes (BSL-23, responder status) will be tested in a fixed hierarchical sequence to control the family-wise error rate across outcomes: BSL-23 is the primary outcome and is tested first; the responder analysis is only interpreted confirmatorily if the BSL-23 omnibus test is significant. Otherwise, the responder analysis will be reported as exploratory.

Across time points: only T1 analyses are confirmatory. T2 and T3 analyses are exploratory and no further multiplicity adjustment is applied across time points. 

Primary inference (non-directional): confirmation of the primary hypothesis as well as the secondary hypothesis A regarding treatment response is based on (i) the two-tailed omnibus p-value from pmtest(), (ii) conditional permutation variable importance scores together with their rank order, (iii) bootstrap-based 95% confidence intervals for subgroup CATEs in the representative tree (B = 1000 nonparametric bootstrap replicates in which the original tree structure is fixed), and (iv) the calibration and discrimination metrics described in Reliability and Robustness Testing. Subgroup CATEs whose 95% bootstrap CI excludes zero are interpreted as evidence of meaningful heterogeneity.

The secondary directional hypothesis (secondary hypothesis B) is evaluated descriptively only; no formal one-sided test is performed.
table.assumption_violation_model_non_convergen:
A key advantage of using model-based random forests is their inherent robustness to several classical statistical assumptions. Unlike traditional global regression models, this approach does not assume linear relationships between the covariates and the treatment effect, nor does it require a pre-specified functional form for interactions. By employing a non-parametric recursive partitioning strategy, the forest effectively accommodates non-normal distributions and handles complex non-linear dependencies. Furthermore, the use of ensemble averaging across 500 trees mitigates the influence of individual outliers and reduces the risk of model misspecification, ensuring stable and reliable estimates even in the presence of minor heteroscedasticity or skewed outcome data.

The use of model-based recursive partitioning ensures high numerical stability, as the local estimation of parameters within each node is less prone to the convergence issues typically encountered in complex, global longitudinal models. Furthermore, the linear and logistic base models utilized in this framework rely on robust estimation procedures that consistently reach stable solutions within our sample size of n = 530.
table.reliability_and_robustness_testing:
To prevent overfitting and ensure the validity of the identified subgroups, the model-based recursive partitioning algorithm employs formal statistical parameter-instability (score-based M-fluctuation) tests for each split in the representative tree, so that a split is only performed if there is statistically significant change in the model parameters. 

In addition, we conduct a global omnibus test for significant heterogeneity of the treatment effect (pmtest()).
 
Beyond these built-in safeguards, we use two outcome-specific validation strategies, both of which are based on out-of-bag (OOB) predictions from the model-based forest. Using OOB predictions ensures that calibration and discrimination metrics are estimated honestly without requiring an additional sample-splitting step. Both metrics are computed on the complete-case dataset, and their 95% confidence intervals are obtained from the same stratified nonparametric bootstrap (B = 1000 resamples) used for the variable importance scores and subgroup CATEs:

1) Quartile-based calibration analysis (BSL-23, continuous outcome). Each participant's predicted CATE is obtained from the trees in which the participant was not part of the bag (OOB prediction). Participants are then partitioned into quartiles based on these predicted CATEs. Within each quartile, the average observed treatment effect is calculated by re-fitting the ANCOVA base model on the participants in that quartile. Alignment between predicted and observed treatment gains across quartiles supports the calibration of the model. Quartile-specific observed CATEs and their 95% percentile confidence intervals are obtained from the stratified nonparametric bootstrap.
2) Concordance probability for benefit (responder, binary outcome). We compute the concordance-for-benefit statistic (van Klaveren et al., 2018), again using OOB predictions of treatment-specific responder probability, to quantify the probability that the model correctly identifies which of two randomly matched patients (one IG, one CG; matched on baseline BSL-23 within ± 0.2 SD) derives a greater benefit from the treatment. The c-for-benefit statistic and its 95% percentile confidence interval are obtained from the stratified nonparametric bootstrap.
table.exploratory_analyses:
The following analyses are pre-specified as exploratory and will be reported under a clearly labelled heading:
- Stability across time. The full analysis pipeline (forest, omnibus test, conditional permutation importance, representative tree) will be repeated at T2 (6 months) and T3 (12 months) to assess whether the moderating structure identified at T1 is stable over time. Differences in identified top moderators will be discussed but not interpreted as confirmatory evidence.
- Comparison of conditional and unconditional variable importance to characterize the influence of correlation structure among candidate split variables.

Any analyses not pre-specified in this preregistration and not falling under the categories above will be labelled as additional exploratory analyses in the final paper.

This approach combines a parametric base model for the treatment effect with a non-parametric, data-adaptive search for subgroups in which the treatment-effect parameter is unstable across candidate moderators. Both outcomes are analysed separately at the primary time point T1, and the same modelling pipeline is then repeated at T2 and T3 as exploratory sensitivity analyses (see Exploratory analysis).

The analyses rely on two outcome-specific base models, in which the group (treatment) parameter is the parameter of primary interest for partitioning. For the continuous outcome (change in BSL-23 from T0 to T1), the base model is a baseline-corrected ANCOVA, lm(delta_bsl23 ~ bsl23_T0 + group), which adjusts the estimated treatment effect for regression to the mean. For the binary responder outcome, the base model is a bias-reduced logistic regression, glm(responder ~ group, family = binomial(\"logit\"), method = \"brglmFit\"), fitted with the brglm2 package. We chose bias-reduced logistic regression over standard maximum-likelihood logistic regression because brglmFit yields finite, well-defined coefficient estimates even under near-separation conditions that may occur in small terminal nodes with extreme responder rates, while remaining virtually identical to standard maximum likelihood in the absence of separation. Because brglm2 objects inherit from glm, the score function and information matrix used by model4you::pmforest() for parameter-instability testing remain available.

For each outcome, we fit a model-based random forest with model4you::pmforest() using the corresponding base model. The seven candidate split variables described under Measured variables are passed to the forest via zformula = ~ bsl23_T0 + phq9_T0 + gad7_T0 + suicide_attempts_T0 + life_threatening_events_T0 + psychotherapy_T0 + medication_T0. Each forest consists of 500 trees (ntree = 500) grown on subsamples of size 0.632·N drawn without replacement (perturb = list(replace = FALSE, fraction = 0.632)) and stratified by group (strata = group), so that the treatment-arm balance is preserved in every subsample. At each split, three candidate variables are randomly selected (mtry = 3), and partitioning is governed by ctree_control(teststat = \"quad\", testtype = \"Univ\", mincriterion = 0, minbucket = 50, lookahead = TRUE, saveinfo = FALSE). The combination of minbucket = 50 with stratified resampling is intended to keep the treatment-effect parameter stable and to limit overfitting: given the observed arm balance of 52.1%/47.9% (302 IG vs. 278 CG) and the fact that all candidate split variables are independent of group at baseline by randomization, the probability of any terminal node containing fewer than 15 observations in either arm is approximately 0.3% per node.

For each outcome, four sets of results will be reported. First, we test the global null hypothesis of no treatment-effect heterogeneity across the candidate split variables using the omnibus parametric-bootstrap test model4you::pmtest() with B = 1000 bootstrap replicates. To clarify the role of the two resampling schemes in this pipeline: parameter instability itself is assessed at every potential split inside each tree by a deterministic score-based M-fluctuation test on the base-model score residuals, and the ensemble of 500 trees stabilises the resulting variable-selection signal and treatment-effect estimates by averaging over stratified subsamples; the B = 1000 parametric-bootstrap replicates in pmtest() (under which new outcome values are simulated from the fitted base model rather than permuted) are used solely to construct the null reference distribution against which the observed forest-level instability statistic is compared in order to obtain the omnibus p-value. Second, we quantify the relative contribution of each candidate split variable using conditional permutation variable importance (Strobl et al., 2008), computed via model4you::varimp() with conditional = TRUE, OOB = TRUE, nperm = 5, and threshold = 0.2. The conditional version of the importance measure is used to adjust for correlations among candidate split variables, which are expected to be substantial between baseline BSL-23, PHQ-9, and GAD-7 sum scores; for comparison and transparency, unconditional importance (conditional = FALSE) will additionally be reported in the supplement. Third, to obtain an interpretable summary of the moderating structure, we fit a single representative MOB tree to the full dataset using model4you::pmtree() with the same base model and the same zformula, but with testtype = \"Bonferroni\", mincriterion = 0.95, and minbucket = 50. Fourth, for the three candidate split variables with the highest conditional permutation importance, we will produce partial dependence plots that display the predicted conditional average treatment effect (CATE) as a function of each moderator while averaging over the empirical distribution of the remaining variables.

The entire MOB-RP pipeline described above is fitted once to the complete-case dataset for each outcome at each follow-up time point. Specifically, we (i) fit the model-based forest with pmforest() and the corresponding base model, (ii) compute the omnibus heterogeneity p-value with pmtest() (B = 1000 parametric-bootstrap replicates), (iii) compute conditional permutation variable importance scores with varimp(), and (iv) fit a single representative MOB tree to the complete-case dataset with pmtree() (testtype = \"Bonferroni\", mincriterion = 0.95, minbucket = 50). The omnibus p-value from pmtest(), the point estimates and rank order of the conditional permutation importance scores, and the representative tree are read directly from this single fit.

To attach uncertainty to the importance scores and to the subgroup treatment effects without relying on distributional assumptions, we use a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples participants with replacement, stratified by randomization arm to preserve the arm balance (B = 1000 bootstrap resamples). In each bootstrap resample we (a) refit the forest and recompute the conditional permutation variable importance scores, and (b) re-estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) within each subgroup defined by the representative tree fitted on the original complete-case dataset. The tree structure is defined once on the original complete-case data and held fixed; the bootstrap re-evaluates these fixed subgroups so that the reported subgroup CATEs and their 95% confidence intervals reflect sampling variability while keeping the interpretation anchored to a single, reportable tree. For each importance score and each subgroup CATE, the 95% confidence interval is obtained from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its bootstrap distribution. As a stability summary, we additionally refit the representative tree in each bootstrap resample and report the empirical frequency with which each candidate split variable is selected at the root split.

Fallback for computational cost. The pre-specified pipeline (per outcome and per follow-up time point: one 500-tree forest, a 1,000-replicate pmtest(), and a 1,000-resample stratified nonparametric bootstrap in which the forest is refit and the conditional variable importance recomputed) is computationally demanding, and we will run it as specified whenever feasible on the available compute. If the analysis proves computationally intractable in practice, we will apply, in a single pre-specified step, the following reduction: ntree is lowered from 500 to 200, the number of parametric-bootstrap replicates B in pmtest() is lowered from 1,000 to 200, and the number of nonparametric bootstrap resamples is lowered from 1,000 to 500. All other settings (mtry, perturb, strata, the ctree_control parameters, and minbucket) remain unchanged, as does the pooling of bootstrap percentile confidence intervals. If this fallback is triggered, it is applied consistently to both outcomes and to all follow-up time points, and its use is transparently reported in the final paper.

All analyses will be performed in R (≥ 4.4) using the packages model4you (≥ 0.9-8) (Seibold et al., 2019), partykit (Hothorn & Zeileis, 2015), brglm2 (Kosmidis, 2017), and ggplot2 (Wickham, 2011). The forest fitting and the nonparametric bootstrap will be parallelised across cores to keep the pipeline tractable. text.text: The digital therapeutic priovi has small average effects for borderline personality disorder (BPD).
In this preregistered secondary analysis, we aimed to explore the heterogeneity and potential moderators of these effects.
Adults received priovi plus treatment as usual or treatment as usual alone.

At the 3-month primary endpoint (N = 528), model-based recursive partitioning showed heterogeneous effects on Borderline Symptom List-23 (BSL-23) change (p = 0.022) and on clinically relevant response (p = 0.007).

Benefit was larger at higher baseline symptom load: a representative tree split on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 at a score of 23, and the higher-score subgroup had roughly twice the BSL-23 reduction (conditional average treatment effects -0.40 versus -0.19).
Baseline BSL-23, depressive symptoms, and recent life-threatening events ranked as the leading moderators.
Quartile calibration of predicted CATEs was weak and non-monotonic.
The moderators are hypothesis-generating and should not guide patient selection without external validation.

Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a common and burdensome condition associated with pronounced emotional instability, interpersonal difficulties, self-harm and elevated suicide risk, as well as substantial functional impairment and high healthcare costs 1, 2 .

text.text: Evidence-based psychotherapies exist but are resource-intensive and not universally accessible, motivating scalable digital interventions to bridge treatment gaps.
priovi is a self-guided digital therapeutic based on schema-therapy principles, designed as an add-on to routine care.

In the EPADIP-BPD randomized controlled trial, adding priovi to treatment as usual (TAU) produced a small average reduction in borderline symptom severity relative to TAU alone at the primary 3-month endpoint 3 .
text.formatted: In the EPADIP-BPD randomized controlled trial, adding priovi to treatment as usual (TAU) produced a small average reduction in borderline symptom severity relative to TAU alone at the primary 3-month endpoint <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: As is typical for complex psychosocial and digital interventions, this average may obscure meaningful variation in individual benefit.
Understanding for whom a digital intervention works is central to precision mental health care.
The central question in precision health care is "what works best for whom".
Addressing this question is relevant for patients, therapists, and the society.
For an individual patient, it is important to know whether she:he with her:his individual characteristics will benefit from a digital intervention or not.

If no benefit is expected, patients can save time and resources by skipping digital interventions without expected benefit for them and select and engage in digital interventions with a high probability of treatment success.

Therapists also want to know if their individual patients will have a benefit from a digital intervention and whether they should recommend or prescribe a digital intervention to their individual patients.

In societies with public reimbursement for empirically evaluated digital interventions, as for example in Germany for "DiGAs", it is also of high financial relevance to know which patients with which characteristics benefit from a DiGA or not.
Identifying the specific patient characteristics for which an intervention works most is challenging as there are potentially endless characteristics of patients that might be relevant to consider.

Most of the past research, therefore, selected clinically relevant variables that might statistically moderate the effect of an intervention on the outcome to identify subgroups of patients with more or less treatment success 4, 5 .
text.formatted: Most of the past research, therefore, selected clinically relevant variables that might statistically moderate the effect of an intervention on the outcome to identify subgroups of patients with more or less treatment success <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Yet, traditional one-moderator-at-a-time subgroup analyses are underpowered, prone to false positives under multiplicity, and unable to capture combinations of characteristics that jointly shape benefit.

Model-based recursive partitioning (MOB-RP) and its ensemble extension, the model-based random forest, address these limitations by pairing a parametric treatment-effect model with an algorithmic search for regions of the moderator space in which that parameter shifts 6, 7 , producing interpretable, individualized estimates while guarding against overfitting.

text.text: In this preregistered secondary analysis of EPADIP-BPD, we applied MOB-RP to identify baseline characteristics that moderate the benefit of priovi on (i) change in BSL-23 and (ii) the probability of a clinically relevant response at the primary 3-month followup.

We asked: (1) whether the treatment effect is heterogeneous; (2) which of seven prespecified candidate moderators are most influential; and (3) whether higher baseline psychopathology is associated with larger absolute benefit.
Analyses at 6 and 12 months were prespecified as exploratory.
The confirmatory T1 analysis sample comprised 528 participants with an observed BSL-23 outcome at three months (263 control, 265 intervention).

text.text: The confirmatory analysis of change in BSL-23 at T1 was based on N = 528 participants.
The omnibus test rejected the global null of a homogeneous treatment effect (p = 0.022), supporting the primary hypothesis of treatment-effect heterogeneity.

By conditional permutation importance, the most influential moderators were Baseline BSL-23, Baseline PHQ-9, and Life-threatening events (3 months) (Table 2), identifying baseline psychopathology as the dominant class of moderators.

text.text: This split was the most stable feature of the analysis: Baseline PHQ-9 was selected as the root moderator in 70% of bootstrap trees.

Notably, the single sharpest split point was thus defined by baseline depressive symptoms rather than by baseline BSL-23 itself, even though baseline BSL-23 ranked among the most important moderators overall.

The directional secondary hypothesis (that higher baseline psychopathology is associated with larger absolute benefit) was supported descriptively, as the subgroup defined by higher baseline depressive symptoms showed the larger reduction in BSL-23.

text.text: Individual-level discrimination was limited: the concordance-for-benefit statistic was 0.47, close to the 0.5 chance level, indicating that the model did not reliably rank patients by their benefit from priovi.
Even so, Baseline BSL-23 was the most frequent root moderator across bootstrap trees (83%).
The concordance-for-benefit statistic was 0.51.

For treatment response, baseline BSL-23 was the most stable moderator across all three time points, selected at the root of bootstrapped trees in 66%, 76% and 83% of resamples at T1, T2 and T3, respectively.

As at T1, baseline symptom severity (baseline BSL-23 and PHQ-9) dominated the conditional importance rankings for the continuous outcome, and where an interpretable subgroup emerged the larger benefit again fell to patients with higher baseline severity, consistent with the directional secondary hypothesis.

The exploratory analyses also revealed limits to this pattern: at some time points the omnibus test was significant while no single split survived the representative tree's Bonferroni threshold; subgroup estimates were imprecise with widely overlapping confidence intervals; and individual-level validation remained weak (concordance-for-benefit near 0.50).
By the 12-month follow-up the subgroup treatment effects were close to zero with confidence intervals including zero, in line with an intervention benefit that attenuates over time.
These time points were prespecified as exploratory and are not interpreted confirmatorily.

text.text: Adding priovi to treatment as usual produced a heterogeneous rather than a uniform benefit at the three-month endpoint.

For borderline symptom severity, the global test of heterogeneity was significant (p = 0.022), and both the representative tree and the bootstrap root-split frequency identified baseline depressive symptoms as the most stable moderator, whereas conditional variable importance ranked baseline BSL-23 highest; both findings point to baseline symptom severity as the central axis of moderation.
Patients with a higher baseline symptom load showed the larger absolute reduction in BSL-23, consistent with our directional hypothesis.

For clinically relevant response the heterogeneity test was likewise significant (p = 0.007) and baseline BSL-23 was the dominant, highly stable moderator, but the resulting subgroups differed mainly in their baseline probability of responding rather than in the absolute benefit derived from priovi.

Across both outcomes, predictive performance was weak: quartile calibration for BSL-23 change was non-monotonic and the concordance-for-benefit for response was close to chance, indicating that, although moderation is detectable at the group level, the present model is not ready to guide individual-level treatment decisions.

Exploratory analyses at 6 and 12 months were broadly consistent in identifying baseline symptom severity as the recurring moderator, most stably for treatment response, but the subgroup structure became less clearly defined and the treatment benefit . attenuated toward the 12-month follow-up, underscoring that these moderators are hypothesis-generating and require prospective external validation.
In the main EPADIP-BPD trial, adding priovi to treatment as usual produced only a small average reduction in borderline symptom severity at the three-month endpoint 3 .

text.text: This modest average effect is consistent with the broader treatment literature for BPD, in which even established face-to-face psychotherapies such as dialectical behavior therapy and psychodynamic approaches produce only small to moderate effects that are frequently unstable at follow-up 8, 9 .

text.text: It also aligns with the emerging evidence on digital interventions for BPD, where benefits have been shown for specific targets such as suicidal ideation but not consistently for overall symptom severity 10, 11 .

text.text: Our analysis qualifies this average: the benefit was not uniform but was concentrated among patients with higher baseline symptom severity, in whom the estimated reduction in BSL-23 was approximately twice as large.
A pattern in which more severely affected patients derive larger absolute benefit, having more room for improvement, has been described for other psychological and digital interventions 12 .

text.text: In particular, an individual-patient-data network meta-analysis of internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for depression identified baseline severity as the most important modifier of relative efficacy, with larger benefits at higher baseline severity 13 , closely paralleling the severity gradient we observed for priovi.

text.text: Importantly, in the binary responder analysis higher baseline severity was also associated with a higher baseline probability of response, so part of the apparent moderation reflects differences in baseline prognosis rather than in the treatment benefit itself, a distinction between prognostic (risk) modeling and effect modification 14 that is central to predictive approaches to treatment-effect heterogeneity 15,16   .

text.text: Finally, the weak out-of-bag calibration and near-chance concordance-for-benefit we observed are consistent with broader concerns that reliable individual-level treatment-benefit prediction is difficult to achieve in single trials of moderate size 18.

text.text: Our analysis has several strengths.

First, it followed a preregistered protocol, which fixed the outcomes, candidate moderators, and analytic strategy in advance and thereby kept the confirmatory three-month analysis clearly separate from the exploratory follow-up analyses, reducing the risk of data-driven or selective reporting.

Second, rather than testing one candidate moderator at a time, we used a data-adaptive approach (model-based recursive partitioning and model-based forests) that weighs many baseline characteristics jointly and lets the data determine which of them, and in what combination, modify the treatment effect, while built-in complexity control guards against overfitting.

Third, we assessed predictive performance honestly: calibration and the concordance-for-benefit were estimated on out-of-bag observations that had not contributed to the trees generating a given prediction, so they reflect genuine out-ofsample behavior rather than in-sample optimism.

Fourth, we quantified uncertainty with a distribution-free bootstrap, obtaining subgroup confidence intervals that do not depend on parametric assumptions about the shape of the treatment-effect distribution.
These strengths are balanced by several limitations that temper our conclusions.

Because the analyses were complete-case in the presence of differential dropout, their validity rests on the assumption that missingness is conditionally ignorable, that is, missing at random given the observed baseline variables and randomization arm; if unmeasured factors jointly drive both dropout and outcome, the estimates could be biased in ways the present design cannot rule out.

Statistical power adds a further constraint, as the study was adequately powered only for moderate heterogeneity (standardized subgroup differences of about d ≥ 0.35) and underpowered for smaller but potentially meaningful differences in benefit, so the absence of a given moderator signal cannot be read as firm evidence that no such moderation exists.
A second set of caveats concerns how the severity signal should be interpreted.

The candidate moderators were baseline characteristics that were observed rather than manipulated, and although randomization renders the average treatment effect unconfounded, the association between a moderator and the magnitude of benefit is itself observational and may be confounded by unmeasured correlates of baseline severity.

This is compounded by the construction of the responder outcome, which combines a reliable-change criterion with a shift to a less severe severity grade and uses baseline BSL-23 both as the reference for change and as a candidate moderator; together these features can make baseline severity mechanically influential and should be borne in mind when interpreting its prominence.

Precision was a further concern: the subgroup with the largest benefit at T1 was small (n = 60) and its confidence interval wide, while calibration and the concordance-for-benefit indicated poor individual-level discrimination, so the moderation is best regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than clinically actionable.

The same caution applies to the later time points, where analyses beyond the primary endpoint were exploratory and multiple and the attenuation of effects by twelve months coincided with degenerate representative trees, limiting their interpretation.

One prespecified moderator, suicide attempts in the previous three months, was too rare (reported by only 6.4% of participants) to yield an admissible split in any tree, so its zero variable importance reflects a lack of statistical resolution for a low-prevalence variable rather than a moderator that was evaluated and excluded.

Finally, because the findings derive from a single trial with differential dropout and were not externally validated, their generalizability remains uncertain 16, 19 . priovi is a low-threshold, scalable, and low-risk digital add-on to standard care, and our results speak to how confidently it can be offered across the range of patients seen in practice.

text.text: Baseline symptom severity was the most consistent signal across outcomes and time points, and patients with a higher baseline symptom load showed the largest absolute reduction in BSL-23.

Because more severely affected patients often carry the greatest unmet need and can be harder to reach with resource-intensive care, it is encouraging that a self-guided digital option appears to benefit them at least as much as others.
This lends additional support to offering priovi broadly as a complement to standard treatment, with particular promise for patients presenting with greater baseline severity.

These implications remain provisional: individual-level calibration was weak, concordance-for-benefit was close to chance, and the subgroup benefit attenuated by twelve months, so the results do not yet support tailoring treatment to individual patients.
Baseline severity, like any other candidate moderator, would need to be confirmed prospectively and validated in independent samples before it could formally inform clinical practice 20, 21.
text.formatted: Baseline severity, like any other candidate moderator, would need to be confirmed prospectively and validated in independent samples before it could formally inform clinical practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref>.

text.text: In this preregistered secondary analysis, the three-month benefit of priovi was heterogeneous and most pronounced in patients with higher baseline symptom severity, yet validation of the predicted treatment effects was weak and the effect attenuated by twelve months.
Baseline severity is thus a promising but not yet actionable moderator.

More broadly, this first preregistered heterogeneity analysis of a digital therapeutic for BPD shows that group-level moderation can be detected while reliable prediction of treatment benefit remains out of reach in a single trial of moderate size.

Realizing the promise of personalized digital care will require prospective external validation in larger, ideally multi-site samples, and evaluation of the clinical utility of acting on such predictions, before baseline severity or any other moderator can guide patient selection.

text.text: Baseline covariate.
For the BSL-23 outcome, the baseline BSL-23 mean item score entered the base model as a covariate to adjust for regression to the mean.

Seven prespecified baseline variables were supplied as candidate moderators: (i) baseline BSL-23, (ii) baseline PHQ-9 25 , (iii) baseline GAD-7 26 , (iv) number of suicide attempts in the three months before baseline, (v) number of life-threatening events in the three months before baseline, (vi) psychotherapy status at baseline (1/0), and (vii) medication status at baseline (intake of sedatives or antidepressants; 1/0).

text.text: Medication status was derived from recorded Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) codes as any regular or as-needed intake of an agent classified under N06A (antidepressants) or N05C (hypnotics/sedatives).

Baseline BSL-23 enters in two roles (as a covariate in the BSL-23 base model and as a candidate moderator) so that partitioning can detect moderation by baseline severity; splitting responds to instability in the treatment-effect parameter itself (detected via the score function), not to its average level.
We used complete-case analysis throughout: for each follow-up we included only participants whose outcome at that time point was observed, and we did not impute missing outcomes.
Because complete baseline data were a prerequisite for randomization, inclusion is governed solely by outcome availability.
Dropout differed between arms (higher under the intervention).

Following our preregistered plan, we used model-based recursive partitioning (MOB-RP) and model-based random forests to identify combinations of baseline characteristics that jointly modify the effect of priovi 6, 7 .

text.text: Both outcomes were analyzed separately at the primary 3-month endpoint (T1).
The same procedure was repeated at 6 and 12 months (T2 and T3) as exploratory analyses.
The primary analyses were complete-case: participants without an observed follow-up BSL-23 at the relevant time point were excluded.

As a robustness check against differential dropout, we repeated the two T1 analyses after a single stochastic imputation of follow-up BSL-23 (predictive mean matching, fitted separately within each randomization arm, one completed dataset, seed 1234); the binary responder was derived from the imputed BSL-23 using the same definition as in the primary analysis.
Full single-imputation results confirm the complete-case analysis and are reported in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Tables 7 8 9 10 11).

text.text: The complete-case analysis remains the primary analysis.
Base models.
For each outcome we specified a simple model whose treatment-effect parameter was the target of partitioning.
For the continuous outcome this was a baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA-type) linear model of the change in BSL-23, with baseline BSL-23 as a covariate.

For the binary responder outcome it was a logistic model estimated with bias reduction, which keeps the treatment-effect estimate finite even in small subgroups while remaining virtually identical to maximum likelihood otherwise.

Model-based recursive partitioning then searched the seven prespecified baseline moderators (baseline BSL-23, PHQ-9, GAD-7, suicide attempts, life-threatening events, current psychotherapy, and current medication) for cut-points across which the model parameters changed.
Because this instability is assessed over the whole score vector of the base model, a split can reflect a difference in the size of the treatment benefit, a difference in baseline prognosis, or both.
Forest, omnibus test, and variable importance.
To estimate this heterogeneity robustly, we aggregated 500 such trees into a model-based random forest.

Each tree was fitted to a group-stratified subsample of 63.2% of observations drawn without replacement; at each split, three candidate moderators were considered at random, with a minimum of 50 observations per terminal node.
We tested the global null hypothesis that the treatment effect does not vary with any baseline characteristic using a parametric-bootstrap permutation test with 1000 replicates.

We ranked the moderators by conditional permutation variable importance 17 , which evaluates each moderator within strata defined by the remaining moderators and therefore reflects its contribution conditional on the others.

text.text: The omnibus heterogeneity test used a parametric-bootstrap permutation procedure (B = 1000) based on score contributions from the base model and therefore does not depend on residual normality of the linear BSL-23 model.
For the binary outcome, bias-reduced logistic regression was used to avoid infinite estimates in small subgroups.
Representative tree, subgroup effects, and partial dependence.

For interpretability we fitted a single representative tree with the same base model and the same seven moderators, Bonferroni-corrected split tests across those moderators (minimum criterion 0.95), and a minimum of 50 observations per terminal node.
For each terminal subgroup we report the conditional average treatment effect (CATE): the group coefficient for the continuous outcome and a g-computation risk difference for the binary outcome.

For the three most important moderators we also visualized how the predicted effect varied across the moderator, averaging over the observed distribution of the remaining moderators (partial-dependence profiles; Supplementary Fig. 1 2 3 4 5 6).

text.text: Uncertainty for the importance scores and the subgroup CATEs was obtained from a stratified nonparametric bootstrap (1000 resamples with replacement within arm).
The tree structure was fixed on the original data and re-evaluated in each resample; 95% confidence intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.
We also recorded how often each moderator defined the first split of a tree refitted in each resample.
For the continuous outcome we assessed calibration by grouping out-of-bag predicted CATEs into quartiles and comparing them with the observed treatment effect in each quartile.
For the binary outcome we computed the concordance-for-benefit statistic from out-of-bag predictions 15 .
Both metrics used the same stratified bootstrap.
All confirmatory tests were two-sided at α = .05.
The two outcomes were tested hierarchically, BSL-23 first, with the responder analysis interpreted confirmatorily only if the BSL-23 omnibus test was significant and exploratorily otherwise.
Only the T1 analyses were confirmatory.
Subgroups whose 95% CI for the CATE excluded zero were interpreted as evidence of meaningful heterogeneity; the directional secondary hypothesis was evaluated descriptively.
